chain.g: to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield on the arm; to grasp (a shield or spear); to acquire, take hold of; to receive; to undertake; to affect, influence; to incite; to unlawfully influence a jury; to surround; to conceal, cover; to shelter; to protect; to comfort; to comprehend, understand

ety.text: The verb is derived from Middle English embracen (“to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield on the arm; to grasp (a shield or spear); to acquire, take hold of; to receive; to undertake; to affect, influence; to incite; to unlawfully influence a jury; to surround; to conceal, cover; to shelter; to protect; to comfort; to comprehend, understand”) [and other forms], from Old French embracer, embracier (“to kiss”) (modern French embrasser…

senses.d: To clasp (someone or each other) in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.
ex: I will imbrace him with a ſouldiour's arme, / That he ſhall ſhrinke vnder my curteſie, […]
And after the vprore was ceaſed, Paul called vnto him the diſciples, and imbraced them, & departed, for to go into Macedonia.

senses.d: To seize (something) eagerly or with alacrity; to accept or take up with cordiality; to welcome.
ex: I wholeheartedly embrace the new legislation.
Embrace any opportunities that may come your way.

senses.d: To submit to; to undergo.
ex: What I haue done my ſafety vrg'd me to: / And I embrace this fortune patiently, / Since not to be auoided it fals on me.

senses.d: To encircle; to enclose, to encompass.
To enfold, to include (ideas, principles, etc.); to encompass.
ex: Natural philosophy embraces many sciences.
Not that my ſong, in ſuch a ſcanty ſpace, / So large a Subject fully can embrace: […]

senses.d: To fasten on, as armour.
ex: VVho ſeeing him from far ſo fierce to pricke, / His warlike armes about him gan embrace, / And in the reſt his ready ſpeare did ſticke; […]

senses.d: To accept (someone) as a friend; to accept (someone's) help gladly.
ex: He bears himſelfe more proudlier, / Euen to my perſon, then I thought he would / When firſt I did embrace him.

senses.d: To attempt to influence (a court, jury, etc.) corruptly; to practise embracery.
An act of putting arms around someone and bringing the person close to the chest; a hug.
ex: [A] long and affectionate embrace supplied the place of language in bidding each other adieu; […]

[…] And tears are on the mother’s face,
⁠As parting with a long embrace
She enters other realms of love; […]

senses.d: An enclosure partially or fully surrounding someone or something.
ex: When he reached the ridge the outlying fog crept across the summit, caught him in its embrace, and wrapped him from her gaze.
We were now within the embrace of a broad bay flanked on either hand by a low promontory.

senses.d: Full acceptance (of something).
An act of enfolding or including.
